dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Stripe wire contract

evidence.note: Planning prose describes building 'all required endpoints, auth, idempotency, webhook delivery, and the PaymentIntent state machine' straight from the spec's route table — no attempt to establish Stripe's actual object shapes, ID prefixes, or SDK expectations before coding.

Dependency installs are only starlette/uvicorn/httpx/python-multipart. The agent never installs or imports the real `stripe` SDK, so it never grounds responses against how the SDK parses them — coding to a guessed contract.

Verification plan lists curl tests of endpoints ('test card declines', 'idempotency') but exercises them by hand via curl, not through the SDK; no derivation of the published test PAN set or decline codes is visible anywhere.

Final self-assessment merely enumerates that the code 'includes all required functionality' (a paraphrase of the spec) with no reference to verified wire shapes, SDK round-trips, or resolved contract ambiguities — confirming no reverse-engineering occurred across the full arc.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built the API essentially from the spec's route table, echoing spec terms (error envelope, state machine) without independently establishing Stripe's real wire contract — it never installs or consults the `stripe` SDK, never derives the test-PAN set, event strings, or scope semantics, and never verifies deserialization. That matches the level-3 anchor ('reads the spec table, recalls a few fields from memory, never checks the SDK') but falls slightly short since even the recalled details are generic and spec-sourced rather than Stripe-specific, placing it at a 2.

dimensions.name: Decomposing the surface into sequenced, checkable milestones

evidence.note: Initial plan enumerated all components (auth, idempotency, webhooks, state machine, all endpoints) and sequenced work as requirements→main code→entry point — a flat build plan, not milestones with done-conditions.

Showed shared-machinery-first thinking: wrote infrastructure/utilities/auth/idempotency/webhooks/pagination before route handlers, then create_app with billing worker. But the three tricky subsystems were folded into generic 'append the route handlers' chunks with no completion criteria or risk-based sequencing.
Rewrote entire __init__.py in one generator script — a single undifferentiated push producing all resources at once, rather than incrementally verifiable milestones.
From ~step 14 through the end the agent was consumed by terminal-recovery thrashing; no milestone structure was maintained, refined, or used to steer the remaining work.
Trajectory ends with repeated 'Mark task complete' submits amid a broken terminal — no milestone hierarchy ever guided execution to closure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a flat, resource-enumerating build plan with a mild foundation-first instinct (infra/auth/idempotency utilities written before route handlers), which lifts it above the pure level-3 anchor. But it attached no concrete done-conditions to items, never isolated the three hard subsystems (state machine, webhooks, idempotency) as their own risk-prioritized milestones, and produced everything in one undifferentiated generator-script push, falling well short of the level-5 'foundation → CRUD → tricky subsystems with completion criteria' plan. This places it at a 4 — between the flat-list anchor and a sensible milestone plan.

dimensions.name: Designing an SDK-driven, offline verification loop

evidence.note: Boots via start.sh and confirms GET /v1/health returns {"status":"ok"} — the one verification that actually succeeded; also fixed a Starlette on_event boot error found by running it.

A handful of manual curl calls to /v1/customers and /v1/payment_methods with a stated plan to test idempotency, declines, and auth errors — but the calls fail (missing python-multipart) and the tricky-behavior tests are never actually executed.

Writes repeatable test scripts (check.py, setup_and_test.py, full_setup.sh) intended to set up + test endpoints, showing intent toward a harness, but output was never visible so no results were ever confirmed.

The overwhelming majority of the run is terminal-recovery flailing after an exec redirect wedged stdout; verification never lands. No stripe SDK is ever used (no import stripe, no api_base) and no tricky subsystem is verified.
Marks task complete admitting terminal output isn't visible and 'the server should be running' — closing without any verified check of the deliverable.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent booted via start.sh and confirmed the health contract (above the bare-curl level 3) and attempted repeatable test scripts covering intended happy paths, but the happy-path curls failed on a missing dependency, no verification used the real stripe SDK, and none of the four tricky behaviors were ever actually exercised or confirmed. Roughly 150 of 177 steps were consumed by terminal-recovery churn, and the run ended by marking complete without any verified result. This lands between anchor 3 and 5 — better than a couple of manual curls, but short of validated happy paths and any SDK round-trip — so a 4.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a broad surface

evidence.note: Only real coverage-tracking observed: the agent noted 'the first two parts of the code are written... now I need to append the remaining handlers' — a rough sense of which resources were done vs. pending during the build phase.

Tested only happy-path curls (create customer/payment method); never advanced to idempotency, webhooks, state machine, or error-envelope checks. Conflated 'server responds' with 'endpoints correct' — the final submit rests on this.

~155 consecutive steps looping on terminal-recovery with the same recycled tactics (kill processes, redirect to /dev/tty, write-to-file, exec bash). Plan text is copy-pasted verbatim across dozens of steps, showing zero awareness that the entire budget was being sunk into one stuck path.

Submitted 'task complete' asserting all resources/subsystems are implemented based on 'was working earlier,' with no verification and full acknowledgement that output had been invisible for over a hundred steps — no accurate done-vs-remaining picture at all.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed a flicker of build-phase sequencing (steps 5-9) but otherwise displayed essentially no situational awareness: it conflated 'endpoint exists' with 'endpoint correct' (step 16, final submit) and repeated an identical failing fix for ~155 steps without ever recognizing the loop or changing strategy — the defining failure of the low anchors. This sits between anchor 0 ('no awareness whether time is being sunk into a stuck path') and anchor 3 ('repeats the same failing fix without recognizing the loop'), landing at 1 because the catastrophic, unrecognized 155-step loop is worse than a typical '3' while the brief early sequencing keeps it just above absolute zero.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting when Stripe's real behavior diverges

evidence.note: Competent local course-corrections to falsified ENVIRONMENT assumptions: switched to a generator script after shell-escaping broke the write; fixed Starlette import then downgraded to 0.37.2 when on_event was gone; installed python-multipart. Real adaptation, but all tooling-level, never the Stripe wire contract.

Only /v1/health was ever verified; the agent never got the SDK exercising idempotency, webhook signing, or the PaymentIntent state machine, so there is essentially no correction of a falsified wire-contract assumption — the heart of this dimension.

After correctly hypothesizing the exec redirect (step 81), it repeated the identical `exec > /dev/tty` patch ~50 times with cosmetic variations, never revising the underlying model or trying a fundamentally different recovery. The same failure recurred for ~100 steps — local patching without revisiting the wrong model.
Submitted 'task complete' while explicitly unable to verify the server was running — barrelling ahead on a known-broken/unverified foundation, the antithesis of disciplined re-grounding.

dimensions.reasoning: Early on the agent shows anchor-5-style competent local reactions to falsified tooling assumptions (Starlette version, multipart, escaping), which keeps it off 0/1. But it never reaches wire-contract verification, so there is no revision of a shared contract/signature/idempotency model, and the dominant behavior — ~100 steps repeating one non-working patch without revisiting the underlying model, then submitting on a known-broken foundation — matches the anchor-3 'local patches, never revisits the wrong model, same class of bug recurs' and even the anchor-0 'keeps building on the falsified assumption.' Weighing the whole horizon, the sustained failure to re-ground outweighs the early local fixes, placing it at 2.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity build: a single-container service that must reproduce Stripe's REST API at the wire level across ~12 resource families so the real `stripe` Python SDK works unmodified. Difficulty comes from (a) a large, interdependent surface, (b) exact contract fidelity to behavior the spec only partially states (ID prefixes, JSON shapes, error envelopes, event types), and (c) three notoriously subtle subsystems — idempotency replay with concurrent serialization, webhook retry/re-signing, and the PaymentIntent state machine. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in orientation, decomposition, and an SDK-driven verification loop, and would sequence the tricky subsystems deliberately rather than sprinting endpoint-by-endpoint.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Stripe wire contract
dimensions.description: Understanding the true target contract — Stripe's object shapes, ID conventions, error envelope, status mappings, test PAN behavior, SDK expectations — before and while implementing, rather than coding to a guessed API.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec lists routes but leaves the exact wire format (field names, ID prefixes like pi_/ch_/cus_, list envelope, event type strings, how the stripe SDK deserializes responses) implicit. Wrong shapes silently break SDK compatibility even when endpoints 'work', so grounding in the real contract is decisive.

anchors.0: Invents an ad-hoc API from the route table; no attempt to establish Stripe's actual response shapes, ID conventions, or how the SDK parses them.
anchors.3: Reads the spec table and recalls a few Stripe fields from memory, but never checks the real SDK's expectations or clarifies ambiguous behaviors before coding.
anchors.5: Establishes the core contract for the main objects (error envelope, list envelope, key ID prefixes, status enums) up front and consults the stripe SDK's shape for at least the central resources before implementing them.
anchors.8: Systematically probes the contract: inspects/derives exact field shapes and ID prefixes per resource, the published test-PAN set and decline codes, event type strings, restricted-key scope semantics, and how the installed SDK deserializes each — building a reference it implements against and returns to as new resources arise.
anchors.10: Sustained, layered reverse-engineering: verifies edge behaviors (error body on idempotent replay of a decline, late-webhook signature windows, capture-on-succeeded state error) against the SDK's actual round-trip, resolves each ambiguity with evidence rather than assumption, and keeps the contract reference authoritative as understanding deepens.

dimensions.name: Decomposing the surface into sequenced, checkable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking the ~12-resource surface plus three hard subsystems into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals — each with a concrete done-condition — and sequencing foundations (auth, error envelope, health, one CRUD spine) before the tricky paths.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is far too large for one undifferentiated push; shared machinery (auth, error envelope, idempotency, IDs) underpins everything, and the state machine / webhooks / idempotency demand dedicated focused effort. Poor sequencing causes rework and half-finished resources.

anchors.0: No structure; starts writing endpoints in spec-table order with no notion of foundations, dependencies, or completion criteria.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of resources with no ordering rationale, no shared-machinery-first thinking, and no explicit done-condition per item.
anchors.5: A sensible milestone plan: shared foundation (auth/errors/health/IDs) first, then CRUD resources, then the three tricky subsystems, with rough completion criteria for the major chunks.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware decomposition that isolates cross-cutting machinery (idempotency middleware, error envelope, restricted-key scoping, background workers) as their own milestones, sequences the state machine / webhook / idempotency subsystems where their prerequisites are ready, and attaches a concrete verifiable done-condition to each milestone.
anchors.10: A living, well-calibrated milestone hierarchy that reflects true risk and dependency: hardest/riskiest subsystems scheduled to de-risk early, milestones sized to remain independently verifiable, and the structure visibly steering execution and being refined as scope realities emerge — without ceremony.

dimensions.name: Designing an SDK-driven, offline verification loop
dimensions.description: Deliberately building checks that the service actually behaves Stripe-compatibly — ideally exercising it through the real stripe SDK pointed at api_base, plus targeted tests for the three tricky subsystems and the boot/health contract — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compatibility failures are invisible without active checking, and the hardest behaviors (idempotent replay of a decline, concurrent same-key non-double-charge, webhook backoff/re-sign, capture-on-succeeded rejection) are exactly the ones a casual smoke test misses. A verification loop is the primary defense over this horizon.

anchors.0: No verification beyond the code appearing to run; never boots the service or checks a response shape.
anchors.3: A few manual curl calls to a couple of endpoints; no SDK round-trip, no coverage of the tricky behaviors, no repeatable check.
anchors.5: Boots via start.sh, confirms health, and validates the main happy paths — at least some via the actual stripe SDK — with a handful of error-case checks.
anchors.8: Establishes a repeatable, SDK-driven check across resources AND purpose-built tests for the trip-up behaviors: idempotent replay returns identical IDs/bodies (including the original error), mismatched-body key → idempotency_error, concurrent same-key serializes without double-charge, webhook retries/backoff/re-signing, and the PaymentIntent state-machine errors.
anchors.10: A comprehensive verification harness treated as the source of truth: adversarial and concurrency scenarios, config-driven timing behaviors (retry schedule, TTL, billing interval) exercised, restricted-key scope enforcement checked, and checks run continuously so regressions surface immediately — verification designed before/alongside the code it guards, not bolted on at the end.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a broad surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across all resources and subsystems, and detecting stuck/thrashing states (e.g. re-debugging the same SDK deserialization or signature mismatch in circles).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints and several stateful subsystems, it is easy to lose the plot — believe a resource is 'done' when only its happy path exists, or loop on one webhook/idempotency bug while the rest rots. Accurate progress tracking sustains forward motion over the horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; no awareness of what remains or whether time is being sunk into a stuck path.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; conflates 'endpoint exists' with 'endpoint correct'; repeats the same failing fix without recognizing the loop.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of resources/subsystems and their rough state, and generally notices when blocked on one area.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, regularly-updated map of implemented-vs-verified-vs-remaining across the surface, distinguishes 'passes happy path' from 'edge-cases covered', and explicitly recognizes and breaks out of circular debugging on the tricky subsystems.
anchors.10: Continuous, evidence-based situational awareness across the whole horizon: tracks verification status per subsystem, catches thrashing early and changes tactic, and reprioritizes remaining work against a clear picture of what is truly done versus superficially present.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting when Stripe's real behavior diverges
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when an assumption about the wire contract or a subsystem is falsified — e.g. the SDK rejects a response shape, the signature scheme is wrong, or the idempotency/state model doesn't hold — rather than pressing on.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Many assumptions about exact Stripe behavior will prove wrong mid-build; the cost of a falsified contract assumption compounds across every resource that shares it. Prompt correction (especially to shared machinery) prevents systemic breakage.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (SDK errors, failing checks) and keeps building on the falsified assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts to individual failures with local patches but never revisits the underlying wrong model, so the same class of bug recurs.
anchors.5: When a check or the SDK contradicts an assumption, fixes it and adjusts nearby code, correcting the immediate divergence competently.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified assumption as a signal to revise the shared model (error envelope, ID scheme, signature/idempotency design) and propagate the correction across affected resources, rather than patching each site — with a brief rationale for the change.
anchors.10: Anticipates and rapidly localizes divergences, re-grounds in the real contract when surprised, and makes disciplined design revisions that prevent whole categories of failure — visibly trading off rework cost against correctness, and never barrelling ahead on a known-broken foundation.
